United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)

title.narrative: Implementation of the 2003 Recommendation Multilingualism and IDIL

description.narrative:
In an increasingly digital world, it is essential to facilitate people's access to the Internet. But today, there are only around 400 languages fully accessible online, representing just a fraction of the world's 7,000 spoken and signed languages. The world is losing its languages—and with them, entire ways of knowing, seeing, and participating in society. Many Indigenous and minority languages are under threat, stripping communities of access to education, justice, health information, and public life, and deepening social inequalities. The rapid digital transformation and the rise of artificial intelligence risk entrenching linguistic hierarchies, leaving marginalized populations voiceless in the technologies that shape their futures. Protecting and promoting linguistic diversity is therefore not a cultural luxury; it is necessary to safeguard the human right to choose and use one’s own language, and it is essential for inclusion, equity, and the preservation of knowledge and cultural heritage in the 21st century.
Objective: Guided by its 2003 Recommendation concerning the Promotion and Use of Multilingualism and Universal Access to Cyberspace, UNESCO, as the only United Nations agency with a specific mandate on multilingualism and linguistic diversity, leads a coordinated and collaborative effort to safeguard and revitalize vulnerable languages, and the implementation of the International Decade of Indigenous Languages (2022–2032).
Key Activities: Working with Member States, academia, the private sector and linguistic communities, UNESCO monitors implementation of the 2003 Recommendation on multilingualism as a normative framework across education, media, science and digital technologies, and—together with ICANN—advances multilingualism online through an MoU promoting Universal Acceptance so all scripts and languages function in domains, email and digital services. UNESCO also leads the World Atlas of Languages (WAL) to fill critical data gaps with an open platform that makes languages—especially Indigenous and low-resourced—visible and measurable for evidence-based policy and integration into public systems and digital environments. To strengthen multilingualism in the AI era, UNESCO convened two global conferences on language technologies and launched its Roadmap on Multilingualism in the Digital Era, guiding inclusive, rights-based approaches to language tech and AI. Finally, UNESCO leads the International Decade of Indigenous Languages (2022–2032) (CI as Secretariat), coordinating the Global Task Force and supporting Member States’ National Action Plans to empower communities to protect and digitally enable their languages through participatory, culturally sensitive, and ethical data practices.
Key Results / Deliverables • Member States are informed, equipped, and empowered to effectively implement and mainstream the 2003 Recommendation concerning the Promotion and Use of Multilingualism and Universal Access to Cyberspace, supported by evidence-based tools, inclusive digital standards, and strategic guidance on language technologies. • Indigenous languages are recognized by Member States within their legal systems and legislation which in turn are supported with comprehensive language-related laws and policy frameworks: more National Action Plans were launched for the International Decade of Indigenous Languages as localized versions of the Global Action Plan of the Decade. • Strategic guidance and coordinated action through UNESCO’s Roadmap on Multilingualism in the Digital Era, supporting ethical, inclusive, and rights-based deployment of language technologies and AI. Universal access and meaningful inclusion for all language communities are advanced while safeguarding cultural integrity and community agency. Digital platform and AI developers are enabled to more reliably incorporate high quality linguistic data into their models and tools in a manner that is respectful of data sovereignty and informed consent, strengthening both the utility and cultural legitimacy of digital systems.
